utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The hearing is resumed. Mr. Registrar, please have the accused brought in. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. I believe that the interpretation booths are ready, they have already worked a good part of the morning, but we are to thank them, we are going to work for about an hour now and continue with the cross-examination of the witness. Does everybody hear? All right then, we can begin. Who will be doing the cross-examination? Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It will be me, Mr. President. MS. ADVIJA HRUSTIC (continued) Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Hrustic, I am Anto Nobilo and together with my colleague Mr. Russell Hayman, we are the Defence counsel for Mr. Blaskic and we have some questions for you. You said that the director assembled all the teachers and said that you would be teaching in Croatian. What does that mean in practical terms, have you changed anything?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have not changed anything really, but the curriculum was the same, but the Serbo-Croatian language which we were using up until then, it was not Bosnian. We could not use, we had to use Croatian, so the curriculum will stay the same, except for the Serbo-Croatian language, that was changed into Croatian language and also the language was changed into Croatian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in practical terms, have you changed the language that you had spoken up until then in your teaching?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Myself, no, I did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I was teaching English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you had to be speaking also in Bosnian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was translating from English into Bosnian, I was told to use the Croatian terminology and we were also using the Croatian text books for English.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now the soldiers with oak leaves who in your phone conversation told you they were from Herzegovina. Could you determine how much in terms of time, how much earlier before this conflict of 20th April were you talking to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think I talked to them some time in November, so they were there since the fall, somewhere around there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This was November 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, when did you stop seeing them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I left Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you saw them throughout that period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were there throughout this period. We could see them, we could observe them. They were accommodated in the Slobodan Princip Selo factory and in the school and we could observe them, we could see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Apart from checking your IDs when you were passing, did you personally see any act of violence on the part of these soldiers with the oak leaves on their arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the checkpoint at our village?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, before that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those men were together with the men who were, say, surrounding the marketplace. We could see them around the town, not in columns, not in big groups, but we could see them together with the HVO military around town.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But apart from the cases when they turned over the stalls on the marketplace, have you noticed any acts of violence towards civilians on the part of these men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A day or two before the attack on Ahmici, and the surrounding villages, did you observe any troop movements, some unusual larger movements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could you describe to us what the location of your hamlet was in relationship to the Slobodan Princip Selo factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what respect?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you in the high ground on the hill immediately above the factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I could see the compound. We were to the left of this factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that your village borders on the fence which is where the compound of the factory begins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could we say that Donje Veceriska, lower Veceriska, over on the other hill, was also adjoining the Slobodan Princip Selo factory?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the examination-in-chief, you told the Prosecutor that there were six to seven soldiers in the village.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many inhabitants did the village have altogether, if you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many households there were in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Altogether there were about 100, that is Serbian, Croatian and Muslim.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many Muslim households out of these 100?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 40 or 45.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the Muslims were not a majority, or were they?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were not. We were pretty evenly split. I do not know exactly, the exact number of households, but it was about even.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many military conscripts there were in your village, men of a military age, I mean approximately?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 30.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the commander of the BiH army units in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nermin Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the deputy commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nihad Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the unit that he commanded, or to what brigade did he belong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was not a unit, it was simply they were just like representatives of the local commune, they were the representatives of our village on military issues. When there were negotiations with the Croats, when we received the ultimatum from the Croats, these people were elected on behalf of the village population to negotiate. They were not part of any unit, they were not part of any military because we did not have any military unit in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Ms. Hrustic, were you on 4th May 1993 -- did you give a statement to the 308th Mountain Brigade of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you say, and I will quote this in English and you will get: "The commanding officer of the unit of the Bosnian army was Hrustic Nesad who was absent and his deputy Hrustic Nihad refused the ultimatum to surrender the weapons."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, but that was in a sense of commander, that is the representative of the Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But here it says, "to the military authorities", you speak about the military authorities and you say that he was the commander of the unit of the Bosnian army, that Nihad Hrustic was that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When you say the Croatian side, you name a name. If you say the Bosnian side, I cannot tell you because I am not a strategist, but I know that we did not have any units there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have a radio transmitter there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was it located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I do not know exactly right now. It was an improvised radio transmitter, because we had pretty good people who were trained in the former JNA to handle these things. In any event, it did not operate because we did not establish any contact.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to read you another portion of the statement that you gave to the military authorities immediately upon your departure from Vitez: "During the attack on the village, the house of Hrustic Mahmut was destroyed. In the house was a radio station and the deputy commander Hrustic Nihad. They were both killed by the grenade which destroyed the house." Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was not a military radio transmitter, this was a walkie-talkie.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who were they communicating with on this walkie-talkie, as you call it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me, how did you get information on the number of rifles in the village? Did you personally enquire about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, this is approximately what I observed, and before the attack on the village, this is what I heard from the men in the village and what we could see, because all these people were very afraid, they had nothing and I could see their makeshift rifles that were turned into military rifles. I also know how many people were going to the front-lines against the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they bringing their weapons back to the village or rifles from the front-lines?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they did, but for the most part the rifles had to be left somewhere behind, I do not know where, I think it was probably in the town of Vitez, in the military command post of some place.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did the negotiations about the surrender of arms start? How many days before the attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was after the burning down of Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was taking part on the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Kadir Hrustic, as far as I recall, because Nihad was killed in the shelter where there were 35 women, so we did not have anybody else so Kadir Hrustic did it and Anto Krizanovic was on the other side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When was Nihad killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nihad was killed the morning when the attack on the village started. He was not in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was he --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry. Nihad and Kadir were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Nihad was the commander or the representative?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Kadir, in what capacity was he there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was an elderly and wise man and we thought of him as having level-headed views and we thought he would represent us in the right way.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the negotiations started on the 17th?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Approximately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there were other negotiations, was that the following day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, the Muslim side again tried to talk. These were calls to lay down arms and for loyalty to Croatia, but our people tried to do something again and were not successful.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us how many days did these negotiations last?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three hours. I do not recall. It was not even a day, it was all within one day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they contact Sefkija Dzidic when they were deciding on whether to surrender the arms or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who decided that the arms would be surrendered, that it would not be surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: People among themselves, the men among themselves, because Nihad and Kadir came with these information and the proposals that were given to them by the HVO side and they would come and explain to the people and then they were all making the decision together.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were giving the statement to the investigators, you said that Nihad Hrustic did not accept the surrender. Do you still claim that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He was the one who told to the HVO that they were not accepting the terms, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there were no weapons in the village, and you could not defend yourselves, why so many negotiations about the weapons and why did you not turn over these few hunting rifles? Can you explain that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we knew approximately what was going on in other villages and we knew if we surrendered the weapons that they would slaughter us, they would kill us, but if we had anything -- if we had anything to defend ourselves with, some could defend the people while the other pulled out the civilians.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Croats with whom you negotiated guaranteed your security, your safety?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In what way?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: During the negotiations; "if you turn over the weapons, we guarantee your safety". Was that mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since the negotiations failed, did they start digging trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Which side?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Your side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not dig trenches. On the very eve of the attack on our village, we had designated a few houses where all the women and children would be, the ones that were closer to the forest and there they dug up some trenches about a metre wide and 1.40 deep. So that is where they were, in front of the houses where the civilians were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am now going to read you another portion of the statement you gave to the Prosecutor: "On 18th April, the Muslims started digging some trenches two to three metres long around the houses, and the able-bodied men started protecting us." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, probably. I do not know, I did not measure these trenches. I can only say they were in front of each of those houses.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night before the attack, you moved to the upper part of the village, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we say that in the lower part of the village, there was a mixture of Muslims and Croats and in the upper part there were Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were mixed in both upper and lower.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were the Muslims represented more, in the upper or lower part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why did you all move to the upper part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because first of all it was closer to the forest and then I saw my first door neighbour and I was socialising with those people up there, and then the lower part was more exposed and we felt that we would be better off if we moved up closer to the edge of the forest.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The night before the attack, did you also spend in the upper part of the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The night before the attack or the night after? You mean the one before that one?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean you expected an attack because you left to go to the upper village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were always hoped that the neighbours would not touch us, because we knew that we had nothing to defend ourselves with, but we saw the surrounding villages and we were expecting something, but we hoped that it would not happen.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, where did you have a clear escape route in the upper part of the village, the upper part of the village, from there, from the upper part of the village, where did you have a clear way out given where the attack of the HVO came?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Towards Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who controlled Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The Bosnian side.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. So between the upper part of the village and the forest and Kruscica, it was open?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, it was just forest, it was our village, the forest and then Kruscica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the men that you describe also withdraw through this forest towards Kruscica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When asked by the Prosecutor, you said that the village was shelled during the attack.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What kinds of shells were they? What did you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact kind of the shells, but I can only describe what kind of impacts there were in the houses. There were rocket-propelled grenades also fired and you could hear very loud explosions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now I am going to read you what you stated to the investigators beforehand: "On 20th April 1993, around 5.00, we heard shells that were being fired in our direction. The shells were like grenades shot from rifles. I know that because their sound is familiar to me and we found some of the shells afterwards which had not exploded." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who set Fikret Hrustic's house on fire, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly who did it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the statement to the military security immediately upon your leaving Vitez on 4th May 1993, you say that Fikret Hrustic was killed and burnt alive set up by Boro Krizanovic, your neighbour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My neighbour came and talked to me about it. I cannot say that he did it, but his words were, "we were in front of Fikret's house, he was inside, he put a lot of pots on against the door and it was ridiculous. We called him out, but he would not want to. He kept shouting and yelling and saying 'this will not be Herceg-Bosna'. He was a fool, he did not need this". Whether Boro meant we -- what he meant by "we" I do not know. I do not know who was there with him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. During the attack on Gacice, who was killed from your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From our village it was -- people had nicknames, so if I do not recall all the names, I apologise. Four civilians were killed. There was a wounded boy, and a couple of wounded women. Fikret Hrustic was killed, Nihad Hrustic, Ekrem Herzegovac, Fikret Herzegovac. I do not know his name, his nickname was Kiko.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That was Ramulj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Ramulj, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nihad, was that the deputy commander? He was in civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He wore a military jacket, but he was in the shelter with women and children, he did not take part in the fighting.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And Herzegovac, do you know where he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Ekrem Herzegovac was fleeing towards the factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He did not die in a trench and killed by a sniper?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he was a civilian, he was very scared and he thought that because he was working in the factory, somebody there would help him and hide him. He started running towards there and he was killed and he had nothing on him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From the four men who were killed, did you personally see how they were killed? Did you actually eyewitness any murder?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not personally. I heard from the people in the village, I did not eyewitness it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Of the civilians, of the people who surrendered to the HVO, after the surrender, was anybody either killed or wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nobody was killed among the civilians. There were some wounded, but among them, there were some wounded ones -- some were wounded later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were taken to the front-lines of the HVO to dig trenches, and Sihad Subasic, who was taken there, to whom I personally took food in the primary school in Vitez, he was wounded in the thigh at Crvene Stijene when he was digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But in the village when they assembled you, when the military entered the village, was there any violence against the civilians there, in the sense of civilians being shot at and wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the lower part of the village, was there a front-line set up, a line of defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to read you another portion of your statement to the military security of the BiH army, where you state: "Already during the first attack, the fighters from the first line surrounded their weapons and they were taken to the primary school at Dubravica."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The front-line, the first line was the man who stayed in that lower part of the village, that first house there. There was a very small trench there, and that was the first or the front-line. When we say the front-line, that was the first position from where the enemy is coming from, where we were being attacked. We had no first, second, third line in our village. There was absolutely no line there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But here you said that the men from the first line, the front-line, turned over the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, from the first lines where the attack came from, that is from their front-lines.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that the men, call it however you like, they turned over the weapons, was it true they were taken to Dubravica to the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were taken to the school in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it correct that one of the men from this front-line, first line, however you call it, Ekrem Hrustic, came with a white flag up to the upper part of the village and called on men to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he came with a white flag up to the village because his brother, who was 15 years old, was lying on the ground and he was wounded. It was three centimetres from his heart, which we learned later. He was not moving, so he came with a large white flag and said, "please surrender, so I can pull out my brother".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he call on all the men to surrender or had they already surrendered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the first men from the lower part of the village surrendered, then Ekrem went to the upper part of the village with a white flag and called on these men to surrender?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He came from the lower part of the village with the white flag and brother was this young boy who was in the upper part of the village, so he came from the lower part of the village up to the upper part.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was he doing up there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He asked the men to surrender.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, and what did he say, who sent him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Hrustic Fadil and his wife Behija and son, who live in the lower part of the village, that they went round the houses looking for people and asking them to surrender because there was no other way out?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that their house was preserved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that Behija Hrustic made a statement on television which was favourable for the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is, and even when we were taken to the hotel she and her husband and the children were the only ones among the Muslims to have stayed behind in the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And nothing happened to them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Nothing happened to them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, in the case of the attack -- during the attack, did you recognise any of the people who were attacking you as your neighbours?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give us a few names of the people you recognised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly all our neighbours, there were Baskarads, Krizanovics, the Bosnjaks, yes, the Matics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So all these families, virtually all the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There were 247 of you civilians in the village, that is what you said, and when you set out towards Vitez two kilometres away, was there any shelling along the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not along the road that we were going on, we just heard very fierce shelling, but where it was I really do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: From what side did you enter Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the side leading from our village past the cinema to the hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And when you entered Vitez, was there any shelling? Were any shells falling?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not see any shells falling, but there was not a soul anywhere. There was virtually no one on the road and I did not see any shells falling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While you were sitting in front of the Vitez hotel, were any shells falling then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, in that part of the area that we could see, no, but we could hear explosions, and a big shell crater was just there in front of the hotel and that is precisely where I personally sat, in one of these craters and behind us, there was a big store and all the window panes were broken, probably from that shell.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when that shell fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, your conclusion that you were used as a human shield, is it based on the statement made by the soldier that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me tell you, the moment that we were brought there with the children and with the men, knowing that there were people dead in the village, knowing a little of what had happened to the other villages, and seeing the fires, the shelling and everything, and what the soldier said, "you sit there for a time and let your people shell you now, because they have been shelling us so far", and knowing that the hotel was a military base for a long time before that day, we could have expected shelling. At this point in time, I believe that we were brought there as a human shield because there were not many Croatian soldiers in the hotel, and then we were taken back. At that moment, at that time, I did not care whether I would die there or somewhere else.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But there was no shelling of Vitez at that time while you were going towards Vitez, when you entered Vitez and while you were sitting there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Gentlemen, it is all the same to you. You can hear it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. The witness has answered that question previously. She said she heard explosions, she could hear shelling; she has answered it and Mr. Nobilo is asking the same question again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: It is not exactly the same question. It is an important point. It is true that one can get lost in many of these details, I can point this out again, both to the Defence and the Prosecution. But the question of human shields relates to the indictment, therefore I think the question has to be asked as to human shields. Excuse me. I think that this is something which must be asked, but try not to ask the question the same way, Mr. Nobilo. My excuses to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I have virtually finished, I just wanted by way of a summary to go through these points; whether there was shelling or not, was it just the personal feeling of the witness. As we were interrupted by the Prosecution, so it has not entered the record. I asked you, when you were going to Vitez, when you entered Vitez and while you were sitting there, was there any shelling, and then we were interrupted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know what was being shelled, I just heard the shells. I do not know which parts were shelled, whether Vitez was shelled or not, I do not know, I just know that I heard the shelling.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Throughout that time on the way there and sitting in Vitez, did you see a single explosion in your vicinity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. How many houses were burnt in your village that you personally saw, and whose houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 35. Believe me, I do not know the exact number, I could not count. They were Muslim houses and one Croatian house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that include the stables?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your previous statement, you said 27 houses.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was a rough estimate, even now I am giving a rough estimate. We did not have time to count the houses, and nobody even cared about houses by that time, we just wanted to save our lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned from Vitez, or rather before that, did they separate the men from the women in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in front of the hotel the men were taken to one side and we were taken in another.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you returned, in how many houses did you live?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In seven.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were they Muslim houses? Was there any food in those houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In some houses there was, in others there was not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any food in the village in the other houses?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean the other Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Or Croatian.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, believe me I do not know how much food there was at the time. No one was hungry, we had to eat, but how much food there was, in which house, I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that you women carried food to the men in the school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is it true that the treatment they were given was decent and if anybody was sick, they were treated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for water, did you have a regular water supply system in the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that everyone did not have water in Vitez at the time because there had been a cut?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that before you left the village of Gacice with your children that some of your local villagers were evacuated by truck. Will you tell me which army evacuated them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before we left the village, after the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After the attack and when you returned from Vitez and when you spent 16 or so days there, at one point you said that some people were taken away by lorries. You later learnt they were taken to Zenica. Who were they taken away by, UNHCR?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were large HVO trucks and there were HVO people in uniform there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were there any UNHCR representatives supervising this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not in our village, I did not see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While the people were climbing into the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did people tell you later that the UNHCR had organised the evacuation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I had not discussed that, so I do not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These men from your village, when they retreated towards Kruscica, do you know what happened to them afterwards, which unit did they join?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I know, 325th. At that time I did not know.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many men joined the 325th unit from the village of Gacice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know the exact number, about 15, 18. I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you mentioned the Split and the Varazdin brigades of the Croatian army, were they units that attacked your village or did you mention them in some other context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Boro Krizanovic told me this, he came that day and said, "you really did not have a chance of defending yourselves because our boys are so good and they are so well trained. They have all come to help us. We have various units, the 125th, the 303rd". I personally did not see insignia indicating 125th or 303rd .

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But he was referring to them as units that had helped them in attacking the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know whether it was in attacking the village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please try to avoid speaking at the same time as the witness is speaking. I am being told that you have to try not to speak at the same time. It becomes too complicated.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We speak the same language, that is why we forget. You said you did not see those Split and Varazdin brigades. Who were you able to see attacking the village? What insignia did they have? What insignias could you recognise and from what distance? When you recognised a soldier with insignia, how far away were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: After the village was burnt down and when the civilians came out of their shelters, the soldiers were there in front of us. We were almost mixed with those soldiers. They were standing at half a metre, they were coming from various directions in the surroundings of those shelters, where all the women and children were. They were all together, the soldiers were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And which insignia did you recognise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HV, HVO, there were some with the sign "U" and the Vitezovi.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many HV insignia did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know. Believe me, I did not count, they were all together, they were mixed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Five, 50? I am asking about the HV?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Objection, Mr. President. She said she did not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you see Darko Kraljevic there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have seen him. I saw him before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see or hear at the time the soldiers reached your village as to whether the HVO had any losses, that any people were killed on the side of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that before the conflict, there were joint patrols, Muslim-Croat patrols in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you do not know. Did the Muslims have their own night patrols?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not patrols, but they had guards.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mean people, stationary guards. Were they armed, these guards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they had hunting rifles. These were mostly older men, pensioners. If they would see more soldiers coming in the direction of the village, they were there to inform the rest. There was mostly one, two on the outside, but mostly one retired person would keep guard duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon? Did you want to ask any additional questions? Re-examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you Mr. President. You were asked a question on cross-examination about when the 247 civilians were assembled and when they walked into the town of Vitez, and you were asked whether there was any violence meted out by the HVO soldiers against the civilians. Do you remember that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we were going towards the hotel, they pushed us, there was the old imam and they put a pistol into his mouth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Ask your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: She answered it in part for me, Mr. President. Just to put it in context as well, were the HVO soldiers escorting you also cursing you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they cursed a lot, mostly --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, I did not ask any questions about the treatment by the soldiers when taking the civilians to Vitez. I asked whether the lady had recognised any violence by soldiers from Herzegovina in the previous months. As for Vitez, I only asked about shelling and that is all.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I disagree with that. I believe the question was asked by Mr. Nobilo as to when the civilians were being escorted into the village of Vitez, whether there was any violence exercised against them. That is what has stimulated this line of questioning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: In general, I would recall the principle that the re-examination must not go beyond the scope of the cross-examination. I think it is no different for the judges. Whether the question of violence, even of verbal violence might not have been asked, but the judges might, so go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, Ms. Hrustic, would you please tell the judges what kind of threats were being made against you as you and the other civilians walked to the city of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were mostly cursing, they were saying that we were balijas, that we were Muslims, that that was not the place for us, that we should go to Iraq, to Iran, some other Islamic countries, that we would all be killed. They would curse our balija mothers, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In addition to that question, when you got to the Hotel Vitez, was there a direct threat made to you and to the other civilians who were there that if you moved away from the Hotel Vitez, you would be killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That happened as soon as we arrived in front of the hotel. The women were very tired, the children were frightened. My eight year old little girl was crying and saying, "please tell the man not to kill us".

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I want to interrupt Mr. Nobilo before he interrupts. Let us not start the examination all over again. You asked a question which I consider was legitimate for the 247 witnesses, but we are not going to begin the examination about things they have already asked. You asked a question which was legitimate, it is time to move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Fine. Ms. Hrustic, you were asked questions about shelling as you were walking toward the Hotel Vitez; could you hear shelling and could you hear explosions from shells while you and the other civilians walked from Gacice to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I believe she answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: She heard that question, it was answered. She said that she had heard the shelling but she did not see any shells falling, so that is a question that has already been asked. Ask another question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I have no further questions. Thank you very much, Ms. Hrustic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. I now turn to you, madam, I am sure that the judges have some additional questions to ask and then everything will be finished. First Judge Riad.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Hrustic. I followed very carefully your description of the events of which you have been an eyewitness. I would like to ask you, just before these events started, was there any threat from the Muslim inhabitants of your village against the Croatian citizens or inhabitants, or did anybody attack Croatian objectives which provoked all these reactions and burning and killing which you detailed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, there were no provocations on the part of the Muslim side. Not a trace of it. We just wanted to live together, to live where we were. We did not even mind the Croatian flags on Croatian houses, we did not even mind the Croatian language that they used. We did not mind, we accepted all that. We accepted it all. Certainly there were no attacks against Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To follow your description of the events during the several days in April, it started with the ultimatum to give the weapons, and you even mentioned -- you mentioned after that that you called the police and the police told you, it was the police I suppose who told you the situation would be solved soon, which you interpreted that they want to get rid of the Muslims. Then you were informed, I do not know who said it, "it is not your country, you have to go to Iraq, to Turkey", and so on. Was that done publicly, in a public announcement or was it just private talk?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I called up the school in which the military were, a long time before that attack, much earlier. We could hear on television, on the radio, representatives of the Croatian side not saying exactly that, "you balijas must go", but they were addressing the Croats rather than the Muslims. They did not address the Muslims in those media. They were saying that their freedom had come, that their age-old aims and objectives were about to be realised, words to that effect. In private conversations with our neighbours or on the phone or talking to other people, we were told that this was not our land, that we should go to Iraq, Iran and so on, that the white line on our flag was pointing the way towards Turkey, whereas the other two sides would be Croatian and Serbian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that your neighbour started practising and having weapons in his house before the events started, if I gathered rightly, and then things started, the shelling, the attack of the village came from three sides at the same time. You also saw the villages around you in flame, Ahmici, old Vitez, Stari Bila, Veceriska. You heard the powerful explosion. In your assessment, did this look like an organised scheme which is simultaneously taking place, especially if they spoke after that, you had a neighbour who told you that, "you have no chance in front of the very good brigades", 303rd and 225th, "because they are so well trained and they are so good brigades". Did you have the impression or did you realise that this was a well disciplined and organised movement, or it was just some unconnected people attacking you from each side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 100 per cent convinced that it was a plan, well prepared and very well organised, because before the attack on our village, a neighbour, a Croat, told me that they had a map of our village, that they had maps of all the localities with exact markings of each Muslim house, and there was not a question of anything being missed, because all that was Muslim would certainly be destroyed. We just hoped that that would not happen, but we knew that if it started that we would not fare well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you went to the Hotel Vitez, that was the headquarters, I think. They put the men on one side and the women on the other side, and you said the soldier said he would go inside to inform the commander. Could you just remind me what was that about? Why did he go inside to inform the commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: He had come with us from the village. We were all together, there were quite a number of soldiers around us, not at every metre, but there were quite a number of them, and he said, "I am going to inform the commander about them", and he nodded his head in our direction and then he went inside to inform him that we were there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he was receiving orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not acting according to his own whim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned trenches being dug and human shields being put in front of the hotel. So all these things were the result of orders?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know why we were put in front of the hotel. I just what I heard the soldiers say.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But the commander was in the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And all this was happening around the hotel?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who is living now in your village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Croats.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But not all the Muslim houses have been burnt?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: A couple of Muslim houses remain, but the Croats have made a list of people that should leave in groups. After I left, my mother-in-law did not want to leave her house, but she was told that all the Muslims had to leave the village, that they would be taken for exchange. That was what they were told, I was not there at the time, and that they had to leave the village.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So the village has become Croat now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just a small detail, you mentioned that on your way, they picked up one of the religious leaders, the imam, and put a pistol in his mouth. Did they choose special people to be persecuted or it was just also done to all the people? Why did they choose an imam?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the man was a Hodza, because he had taught people how to pray, because he was in the mosque and the Muslims went to the mosque.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: You have been a school teacher and I take it that you took some interest in general affairs in Bosnia, am I right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were talking about your being outside the Hotel Vitez with a number of other people, you said the men were separated from the women and children.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps I do not recall it correctly. Can you help me by telling us what happened with the men?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men were taken to the primary school in Vitez, the one I had worked in.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know any of them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Among the captives? Yes, I knew them all, all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, when we took food for them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you took food, did you see them again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the people whom you saw in uniform. You saw some people bearing the insignia of the HV, and the HVO, and the Vitezovi, and some people had an oak leaf. At that time, you regarded President Izetbegovic as the head of the government of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was our President, the Bosnian President, of the Bosnian state.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How did you regard these people whom you described as wearing these insignia? Did you regard them as deriving their authority from the government of Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about the people who demanded the surrender of weapons. They were in uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The same kinds of uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they were locals, they were people from our village who had negotiated before the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they declare to you whether they had any legal authority to demand the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I did not understand the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they say to you that they had legal authority to demand the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you yourself aware of any legal authority which they had to demand the surrender of weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me about those Muslim houses which were not destroyed. Do you have a reason to give the court why those Muslim houses were not destroyed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know exactly why. I think now that it was for them to be able to accommodate us there, or for the Croats who were -- who had moved from areas under the control of the Bosnian army to be put up in them. I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We have completed our work now, it was long, you were extremely courageous and the Tribunal thanks you for having come to The Hague to testify for the Prosecution, but also in service of justice. For the time being, please do not move, the judges will withdraw. The hearing will resume at 2.45. The hearing is adjourned. (1.05 pm) (Adjourned until 2.45 pm) 21 22 23 24 25 (2.45 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. Please be seated. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Before we have the witness brought in, I would like to see where we are as the end of the week is concerned. Mr. Harmon, what is your programme for the end of the week? Today is Tuesday. You had said that you had ten witnesses, I think that you have ten witnesses left, at least that is what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I do not have the list in front of me. I was informed this morning that one of those witnesses now declines to come forward, and another witness will not be called. I get status reports in the afternoons after the session is over, but this morning I was informed, as I say, that one of these witnesses will not be appearing so we will be making some adjustments to the schedule and I am not at a point where I can give you, with any definition, the schedule. Perhaps after the recess this afternoon I will be in a better position to advise your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Perhaps you could let Mr. Fourmy know that, so that we could know how things are going to go. I see that the next witness is protected. In light of what is taking place in this hearing, this might take a bit of time, and I do not think it is wasted time. I noted yesterday two things regarding the two witnesses who spoke. Since this is a public hearing, the protected witness, that is Witness A, whom I consider, I believe that I am speaking for my colleagues, each of the parties played his role properly, we were able to limit the time devoted to the witness. We were able to limit it to the essential questions, both sides asked, as well as the judges, and we were able to have our hearing under conditions which I think comply with the rules in force in this Tribunal. However, unfortunately for the next witness who was partly protected, there we ran into the problems we meet in all systems. There was a summary, there were interruptions which you made throughout the hearing, you asked questions. I am not talking about the cross-examination for the time being, we will get to that when we talk about the Defence. I believe that we tried to continue, always keeping in mind the objective of shortening the trial time, but also -- not only quantitatively but to work in such a way that we could get to the essentials. What I am asking the Prosecutor for the time being is to make the summary, but there is something else I would like to add. I would like you to introduce the witness in terms of the indictment. I have the indictment before me, I would like the representative of the Prosecutor who will work with us to tell us by looking through the indictment what your counts are and what is it you are getting at, so that I might possibly tell you that you are going outside the scope of your role. I would also like interruptions to be as few as possible. We cannot at the same time have a resume and then have questions the way you were asking them and then ask questions again. I think we will never get anywhere doing that and we will extend the testimony beyond what I think is reasonable. I am saying this, but my colleagues as well hesitate interrupting witnesses who are victims, people who suffered during the conflict. It is before the person comes in that things should be settled. You know much more draconian, drastic measures will be taken. Personally, I would like these debates to conserve what you know in your system, because this is a system closer to the common law system and is practised by people working within that system, except perhaps for Mr. Nobilo, who is used to working in another system. Once again, therefore, independent of any measures you will give to Mr. Fourmy by the end of the week, we will take measures next week, and I hope that this next witness will not only be placed within the system you are expecting from the questioning but that it will be part of the indictment which you will have indicated clearly. Say, for example, this is for this or that village which is indicated in the indictment. Other Chambers ask for preliminary statements, we have not reached that type of procedure, because we are not sure that this would produce the results that we are looking for, but the objective of all the Trial Chambers is the same in this Tribunal, that is to have a trial which takes place within a reasonable amount of time and we will be firm about this, as is necessary. I am not criticising you again, I think each person works according to his own legal culture and habits, but once again, we are not common law lawyers or civil law lawyers, but we are judges in an international tribunal, looking for the truth. Now Mr. Harmon, introduce the next witness, who is protected.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President and your Honours, may I respond to your Honour? First off, each of these witnesses that we bring before your Honour we have taken the desires of this Trial Chamber sincerely and we have instructed each of the witnesses to give the court a narrative. Not every witness is capable of giving a narrative and that causes us to ask questions, because oftentimes, as happened with the witness yesterday, the witness answered a question and could not give a narrative. We have to be able to guide the witness through the relevant points of his or her testimony. Mr. President, we have instructed the witnesses to give narratives, we will continue to do so, but we will try to expedite and assist those witnesses when they are incapable of doing so. Mr. President, in respect of the next witness, I will be glad to inform the court and counsel what parts of the indictment this witness will be testifying about. This witness -- first of all, let me give you a summary, Mr. President, and then let me give you the counts of the indictment that we believe their testimony relates to. This witness, Mr. President, is a Muslim refugee from the village of Nadioci. If I could have the ELMO turned on at this point, Mr. President, on the ELMO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you, but I want to take advantage of this time to thank you for what you are saying. I know you are making efforts and you must understand that we are not trying to be polemical in anything we are saying. It is simply for the sake of justice we are working that way, because that is our responsibility. Thank you for what you have just said, I know you are making all possible efforts. My second question is, is this an anonymous and protected witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This witness will be known as Witness S. As I said, Mr. President, on the video screen this witness will be testifying now about the village of Nadioci, so we are moving away and moving to a different village. This village is very close to the Hotel Vitez, and if you look on the monitor, the pointer points to the village of Nadioci. Her testimony will relate to a number of events, Mr. President, that occurred before the attack on Ahmici and on Nadioci. Essentially they relate to the preparations that were made in advance of the attacks on April 16th. She will testify about seeing HVO soldiers filling sandbags, a large number of sandbags, shortly before the attack; she will testify about the evacuation of Croat civilians from her village, and she will testify that she actually received a warning that the attack would occur. She will also testify, Mr. President and your Honours, that soldiers came to her house a number of days before the attack and told her not to leave her house. Shortly thereafter, she made observations from her house of HVO soldiers distributing large amounts of weapons, heavy weapons, artillery, to individuals in and around Ahmici and Nadioci, and she will testify about the prepositioning of those heavy weapons, and actually seeing them firing on 16th April into the village of Nadioci and Ahmici. She will testify, Mr. President and your Honours, about seeing soldiers, large numbers of soldiers advancing past her house on 15th April, preparing for the attack. She will testify about HVO soldiers intentionally setting fire to Muslim residences, and she will testify about a murder of an unarmed civilian by HVO soldiers. Mr. President, the testimony of this witness relates to count 1 of the indictment; that is paragraph 6.1, attacks on cities, towns and villages. It relates to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 6.1, did you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: 6.1, count 1 of the second amended indictment, the persecution count. Her testimony will relate as well to paragraph 6.2 of the indictment and 6.3 of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me, I do not see that here. I have the indictment as it was of 2nd October, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am referring to the second amended indictment, Mr. President. If it is not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Second amended indictment, yes. 6.1 is offences against villages and hamlets, large scale attacks. Do you have that, Mr. Registrar? Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: I am referring to count 1 of the indictment, Mr. President, paragraphs 6.1, 6.2, 6.3, 6.4, 6.5. She will testify about -- let me see if it is 6.6 and 6.7 for just a minute -- paragraph 6.6 and 6.7, so her testimony will be relevant to all paragraphs in that indictment. She will also be testifying, Mr. President, about counts 2 to 4, paragraph 8, referring to the village of Nadioci which is the second village listed in that indictment. She will testify, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, now I am following. I do not find 6.1. I am not going to have you waste any time. 6.1 in the document I have in front of me, 6.1 is widespread systematic attack directed against cities, villages and hamlets, is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We are together now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Continuing on, Mr. President, her testimony will relate to counts 5 through 10, specifically the subpart A of paragraph 9, the wilful killing of civilians. Her testimony will relate to counts 11 through 13, paragraph 10, I am referring to Ahmici and Nadioci. Those are the various charges in the indictment that her testimony will relate to, Mr. President and your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right, then this is a witness for whom you have indicated the counts, I have the French version here, so this is really testimony dealing with preparations that she saw before the attack on the village of Nadioci up to the murder, so you will let her speak and you have understood that you have to interrupt if she is going on too long about something, but when you start up again, I ask you that you remain focused on the essential points in support of the indictment. Very well, we can have the witness brought in now. (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness S, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Registrar -- do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Registrar will give you a declaration which you must make before the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry, I cannot read it because I do not have my glasses. I cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: (Not interpreted) you are going to read it and then say yes you agree or you do not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Or you might repeat. Please repeat. WITNESS S (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. We are going to have your identity verified but please do not say your name. Since you do not have your glasses, perhaps the Registrar will tell you what it says and just say whether it is correct.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand. Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Prosecutor has told you that you were called here as part of the Tribunal's trial, that is for the time being the Prosecutor's case against the accused Blaskic. The Prosecutor will ask you some questions, you will make your statement before the judges, the Prosecutor will ask you the questions which he considers appropriate, and then the counsel for the accused will ask you questions, and then the judges. Mr. Prosecutor, you can begin now. It is 3.05.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Examined by MR. HARMON

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I am going to begin by asking you some preliminary questions. First of all, how old are you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was born in 1937, so I am 60. I am going to turn 61 next.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you married?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you and your husband both Bosniaks who practise the Muslim faith?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before moving to Nadioci in October 1992, were you a resident of Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1992, because of Serb aggression, did you and your husband flee from Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: While fleeing from Jajce, were you seriously injured by an explosion from an artillery shell and did you spend two and a half months hospitalised as a result of your injuries?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your release from the hospital, did you eventually settle as a refugee in the village of Nadioci and did you settle there with your husband?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In 1993, was your husband an invalid who suffered from diabetes and liver disease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: He was not a member of the TO nor the Bosnian army, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The house in Nadioci where you settled, were there Muslims living adjacent to your house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there were also Croats, the locals.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Witness S, I would like to ask you a series of questions and I ask you to give a narrative form of answer to the judge, but let me identify the subject area first. I would like to focus first of all on your observations about significant events that you observed before the attack on Nadioci on April 16th 1993 and specifically I would like to direct your attention to the filling of sandbags that you observed. Will you tell the judges what you saw, and when you saw it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. May I proceed right away? When we came to Nadioci, I was still being treated and I had to go to the medical centre to have my bandage replaced and to receive injections, so about five or six days before this, I saw that some covers or some kind of protection was being put up. They were taking out the sand and these pebbles from the Lasva river, and I was taking coffee to a driver, I had taken him a coffee, he was Croatian, he said, "thank you, ma'am, and be careful". I asked him, "what are they doing with all that sand over there?"; "they are making roads and houses with it", that is what he said.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there Witness S, and let me clarify. When you say "they", who is "they"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Croats, the HVO. The HVO was taking the sand and they had licence plates which said "HVO". This driver told me, "ma'am, be careful". I again went to Vitez to see the doctor and I saw even more of this. They were making these shelters all over Vitez, around the intersections near the hotel, near the cinema, and I saw these machine-guns, machine-guns with bandoleers. I was a bit panicked by the time I got back home and I told my husband, "something is going on", I told him. He said, "it is nothing". I said, "let us run away from here", and he said "nothing will happen", so we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stay focused if I can for a moment on your observations of these HVO soldiers; how many trucks were being filled with these sandbags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Three trucks and they were going in the direction of Vitez and Ahmici. That is where they were taking, that is where they were driving it, because that is what I see on the way back from the city when I passed by.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, how many HVO soldiers did you see loading these sandbags and can you describe those soldiers and what they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about five or six of them who were loading it up and there were another two men in civilian clothes, I did not know who they were, they were loading up this sand and they wore camouflage uniforms. They had the HVO insignia there, there was the chequer board there -- camouflage uniform as they call it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, one last question on this subject, were they load-filling the sandbags and then loading the filled bags on to the truck, is that what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I asked the driver, "when you make the roads and houses, why would you put the sand in those bags?", and he said, "I do not know", but what he told me was, "be careful". He thanked me a lot for the coffee which I had brought him, I had brought him, and he was an HVO but I brought him this coffee.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, to clarify one point, when you went into the town of Vitez to see your doctor, did you see sandbags in positions where you had not seen them before?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Earlier they were not even there, we were passing there. This was when we were coming from Vjetrenica towards Zenica. There were big piles of sandbags with the machine-guns pointing to the Vjetrenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, now I would like to address your attention to your observations in Nadioci in respect of your Croat neighbours. What did you see them do and what did one neighbour in particular tell you? Could you please tell the judges?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I noticed this six or seven days beforehand. They started to take the blankets and some pots, they were going towards where the Croats lived and they were retreating to the upper part and I told my husband again, "something is going on" and he again said, "it is nothing", because he knew I was afraid. Then Djurdja, who was my first door neighbour, she was crying and she said, "take care of yourself, it is not good, hide wherever you can". This is what she told me. The Croats, the locals, they were very nice to us. I have nothing bad to say against them. They even gave us food, cigarettes, coffee, we did not have those things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Shortly after you received that warning from your neighbour, did HVO soldiers come to your house? Tell the judges, if they did come to your house, what they said to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The four men who came, she asked where we were from, I told them -- they saw these refugee cards and they said, "you cannot leave this weekend house", which was right next to the main road, Busovaca-Vitez. They were impudent towards us and one of them turned and mumbled something. I could not understand him. I was afraid. Then they left. Then this Djurdja arrived again when nobody was looking and she said, "run away and go to the woods", and that is what we did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The soldiers that came to your house and told you not to leave, how were they dressed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the camouflage uniforms with the HVO insignia with the chequer board.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After you received those instructions from the HVO soldier and after you received a warning from your neighbour, would you tell the judges what you observed about the distribution of arms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I went to the upper floor of this weekend house to pick up some laundry and two trucks arrived. When they parked in the parking lot, maybe ten minutes later Praga came and they were talking. Praga went across the bridge which was across the river, that is the Lasva river, and they went to the woods and there was nothing coming, no shooting that night. This Djurdja came again to get some blanket again and give us some food and said, "just run into the wood", but we could not flee, we were surrounded, there was no way out, we could not budge. Then when I came out to the door, I saw a Mercedes car. He --
