utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we get to that part of your testimony, I want to stay with your observations about these two large trucks. Could you see any kind of weapons that they were distributing and could you please describe in detail to the judges what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I went to pick up the laundry, I told my husband what had happened downstairs. They were bringing in weapons. I am not a military person so I do not know, but there were automatic rifles there, ammunition, sniper rifles, machine-guns, anti-aircraft gun was taken across the river, and then there was another thing whose real name I do not know, and there were people, they had trousers of the camouflage uniform and they had flak jackets on top and another small group arrived and they all came towards the upper Nadioci. That is where the Muslims lived. Most probably, as far as I could tell, they went to surround Nadioci and Ahmici. In the morning of the 16th, the attack started.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Again staying with your observations of the distribution of these weapons, could you tell the judges who was distributing these weapons? Were these soldiers, were these civilians who were distributing the weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Soldiers, the HVO soldiers, the HVO. They were distributing the weapons and what little was left there, there was some little ammunition, they covered it with canvas canopy and they took it somewhere, towards Vitez they went. We could not see them any more. Ahmici is on the way to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that you saw an anti-aircraft gun being taken some place. Please tell the judges where you saw the anti-aircraft gun being taken.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was taken towards Ahmici, but I know it was that because it is a big thing and in the morning -- I will tell you, we did not sleep much. We saw all this military milling around all night long, there were some in camouflage uniform, some in black uniform, some had the letter "U". They even called themselves Ustasha, this is what we were told.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now let us talk about the night before the attack. You were still in your residence, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the weekend house of the man with whom we stayed. We did not sleep that night, we did not dare turn on the lights. We could see the soldiers passing in groups, and they were split here on this intersection. Some would go up towards the upper Nadioci and the others went towards Ahmici and Vitez. This went on all night long, we were whispering and we would overhear something, but we could not make out the words. I could not hear everything, but they talked on a walkie-talkie and they called the bungalow, because we could hear when he came back and said "bungalow". So there were guards, we were silent all night long, and we were waiting to see when they would come for us, but in the morning, the attack started. When the attack started, the whole land was on fire. We heard shrieks from Nadioci, women and children, so that we could not see who these were, but most probably they were Muslims, because it was a Muslim village. Then we panicked among the refugees, the Muslim refugees and there were some locals among us too. Then we started fleeing towards Dervis Ahmic and we went there to his house and they told us, "do not be afraid of all the neighbours", we feared them not. There was only one, his nickname was Cicko, and he said that he would drink balija blood. He had a big knife or a bayonet. He wore black. I was very scared. There was a Franjo called Svabo. He and his wife came over here, they were Croats, he and his wife and his son. They were all very nice people. They defended us from Cicko. They removed him, but two other HVO neighbours came and they took him away, so that we survived this. Then this anti-aircraft gun kept pounding all day long, and they were using also incendiary bullets. After that, I went up there to look again. I wanted to pick up the clothes, we saw that we needed to run. So this was at Dervis Ahmic. I saw some bodies floating downstream, three bodies, and then there were another three bodies coming downstream. I was too scared and I did not see anything any more. I was just very scared, I had big problems with my nerves and I was in fear. We were still there, there was a Mercedes car that came and it was burgundy with black doors. He came, just turned around and went towards the bungalow and Ahmici. They came back quickly, one person came out of the car, he came to Sefka's home, to the door and I stepped outside. I saw that everything was over. An HVO soldier came in a camouflage uniform, he has a chequer board and the HVO insignia and he is going to her door. I summoned some courage and I said, "she is either not home or she cannot hear". He said to me, "now she is going to hear it". He banged at the door twice and then he kicked in the door and Sefka was at Dervis Ahmic's. When the door was open, he was only there two or three minutes. As he opened the door, thick smoke started coming out and the house was on fire in no time. The house was right next to the weekend house or cottage. We left from there, we told at the Dervis's what had happened. We collected some rags, that is what we call clothes, and we said, "do not worry, there are neighbours here, nothing will happen", so we stayed there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you just a minute, Witness S, and let me get some points, to clarify if I can. First off, the weekend house where you and your husband lived was right next to the road, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and next to the river. The river was just below the weekend house and in front of the weekend house was the main road Busovaca to Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said at one point you went outside and you saw some bodies floating in the Lasva river. How many bodies did you see and could you tell whether those bodies were civilians or the bodies of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were three people tied together, civilian men. They were not women or military men, and when we came to Dervis's house, we were passing through the garden, we did not dare use the road and when we got there, we told him that and they said, "do not be afraid, we have our neighbours here". There was somebody called Slavko, a very nice man, a Croat. He was also a military man from the HVO and he said, "madam, do not be afraid". He said to Dervis, "keep her calm and tell her not to worry". That is what they did. They calmed us down, they gave us sugar and water and then another completely red Mercedes came --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you, because I want to stay on the first vehicle that came to the house. You said a person got out and that person was an HVO soldier. How many other soldiers were with him when he got out and went to Sefka's house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were four of them in all, with the driver. One of them came out and three of them remained in the car on the road. Also this second Mercedes, there were four of them and all four of them came out, but the driver did not come out. We did not see who the driver was. They entered Dervis's house, or rather one of them entered Dervis's house only.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stay at Sefka's house for just a minute, Witness S. Was Sefka a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Muslim. She was over 80. She had no children, she had no one. She was alone, she was a widow. When we got there, Sefka was screaming, she saw the house in flames and she wanted us to put the fire down, and when we came to Dervis's, we came across a man from the Patkovic, from Zenica, and he is a friend of Dervis's.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me turn, if I can, now to the arrival of the second group of soldiers that came after -- okay. How many soldiers came in the second group of soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In this second group there were four, plus the driver.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did they do? Please tell the judges what that second group of soldiers did.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The second group of soldiers, this was still at Sefka's, let me add, and they said, "who are you?", and we said that they were Muslim refugees. They repeated, they said, "you will go with us". But they did not take us, and so we went to Dervis Ahmic, and we had not been there for more than ten minutes when a third group came, four of them plus the driver, one of them came out and the others stood by the car, three of them. This one came in and said, "get out, all of you get out". We all went out and Dervis Ahmic's wife asked whether she could carry some laundry she had prepared in a nylon bag, but the HVO soldier said, "no you cannot take anything out". When we came out, a cat was left, they threw the cat out, then the cat ran back in and he chased it out again. I came up to him and I said, "can we take our things?", and he said, "you can", he did not mind. Then we went out and then he said, "go to Nunga's house", his son's house. This one went into the house and two minutes later, smoke started billowing out of the house and that very moment it burst into flames, and there was nothing we could do. Then another one said, "why do we not go into Ferit's house", which was a house still under construction. This one said, "there is no key", but another one came up and kicked the door open. When we went in, an automatic rifle was fired at us, one bullet passed right by Dervis Ahmic, Patkovic was there, I did not know him, and he is a friend of Dervis Ahmic, and his daughter was there. He happened to be there when the blockade took place, he could not get out, and when these two came, they asked who we were, and then they said to Patkovic that he should follow them. His daughter started crying and the soldier said, "do not cry, he will come back". He was taken from our weekend house, this was 150 to 200 metres, they killed him on the main road, the Busovaca-Vitez road. Then I ran off to the weekend house to collect whatever I could, and to flee into the woods, but some people came, they turned Patkovic around and he was killed, he was killed out of a pistol, I would say. Then they pushed him among some sort of garbage and then these others came and they turned him over. They picked his pockets, but I recognised the man, I was in a terrible state of shock, and when I came up to them, I said -- they asked me why I was in such -- so breathless and I said it was nothing, but I was terrified. When we reached this weekend house, only then did I see that they had thrown the body into the Lasva. This body reached Zenica, they took him out of the water and they buried him in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness S, let me just ask you some clarifying questions. You said you saw some people go into Dervis Ahmic's house and after the person or persons went into that house, the house caught fire. Describe that person to the judges, please, the person who went into the house.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. When talking about these people, I have to say they are the HVO, the Armija was not there, it was mostly the refugees who were in these weekend houses. There were 11 families in all, 17 families.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that Patkovic was taken out by some individuals. Was he taken out by HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO, yes. They took him out, and they killed him, the HVO. The people who came by and who threw the body into the water were also HVO. These were all soldiers, HVO soldiers in Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At some point, did you return to your weekend house and did some HVO soldiers come into your house and do certain things in your house? Please explain to the judges.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came later, four of them. They were not local people, from Croatia, Dalmatia and Skutjure. They are in the borderline between Bosnia-Herzegovina and Dalmatia and we can recognise them by their dialect, the way they speak. They came in and as soon as they entered one of them hit me, my lower dentures fell out. Then they searched our bags, they threw around everything, they trampled on everything, they took my handbag and my husband's bag, all the documents and what little money that we had, some jewellery and my documents, my papers. They took everything and they took it off, they did not give it back to us. They hit my husband two or three times. I closed my eyes, then another one came back and slapped him again, and I said, "you will not get out of here alive". All this was the HVO army. They left, we again went to Dervis Ahmic's, we told him what was happening, then his son Ferit came, they call him Ferdo. We talked, and then his grandson came and he said, "some more soldiers are over there". I went over there, they just asked me where we were from, I said we were from Jajce, they turned around and left. Then Djurdja came, my next door neighbour, she is Croat, and when they left, she cried and she gave food and she said, "watch out, run for the woods".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please tell the judges the circumstances under which you left the weekend houses and eventually arrived in Zenica.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the weekend house, we went to Dervis Ahmic's again, but in the meantime when we went back, this Franjo known as Svabo came, he was making some sort of a list, because allegedly we would be taken to Busovaca for an exchange. We asked him things but he answered nothing, and then he said that he had been -- they had been forbidden to speak to us, and he said that they would come and collect us. In the meantime, this Franjo's son came up, and his wife Zora, and said, "whatever you have, quickly put it in a nylon bag, a van will be coming to take you down town to the school". That school was a camp, but we were lucky, a man from the Red Cross came, he made a list of our names and we were taken into a room, he listed us. The International Red Cross had come, they put us into buses, we had personnel carriers and that is how we were taken to Zenica, and in Zenica there was no food, we were hungry, and so we moved to Travnik. That is where we stayed, in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness S, I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Harmon. I am very sensitive to the form you used which was concise and which I assume allowed you to ask all questions that you wanted. Witness S, I am sure you have been told, it is now the Defence counsel who will do the cross-examination, he is Mr. Nobilo and he will do it. Cross-examined by MR. NOBILO

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, I am Defence counsel Anto Nobilo, my colleague is Mr. Hayman, we are Defence counsel for General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise, I am not testifying against General Blaskic. I do not even know him, I am just saying who the soldiers were, I do not know Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you have never heard of him?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, not until this happened in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you ever see him? Did anyone mention him that evening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no one did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did anyone mention him while you were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mostly it was Kordic that they mentioned.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 300 metres, not more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then Ahmici begins?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The bungalow and then Ahmici.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who was the owner of the house you were living in?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Surely I cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Never mind, it is not so important.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I will remember later.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you were telling the Prosecutor about the truck which came with weapons, where did it stop, in front of whose house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the main road, in the parking area.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In what direction were people carrying the rifles to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In the direction of Nadioci. There is upper Nadioci where the Muslims live.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you saw automatic rifle snipers, ammunition and rocket launchers; how far were you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 50 metres.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This parking area, was it next to the bungalow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the bungalow is further down. The parking area is in the direction of Gornji Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So not on the main road?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on the main road, and then the road goes on to Gornji Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were those automatic rifles in boxes or uncovered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were small rifles, they were under canvas and then they took away the canvas and then there were piles of boxes. They took down the boxes and there were several snipers.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think two or three, I did not see any more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the box?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Probably ammunition, I could not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These small automatic rifles, how many of them were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think they took about 20 and they went off to Gornji Nadioci.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the rocket launcher, what did it look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it looked like this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Could you go slowly, please? Avoid this dialogue which is too direct, because the witness must speak to the judges. I am sure the conversation is very pleasant in your own language, but does not always allow the judges to follow the questions and the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Though some people say it is two languages, still we do understand each other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, indeed. What did this rocket launcher look like?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I could see, it was about this size, so high (indicates). It has several slots for shells and then one after another the shells come out. I saw this in Jajce the same thing but I saw it there also and that is how I know it is a multiple rocket launcher.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How high is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This high, about one metre.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they unload it from the truck?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took it to Gornji Nadioci, and this anti-aircraft gun was taken across the river.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you did not sleep that night; what about your neighbours, did they sleep?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, they did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it obvious that something was in the offing, that there would be a conflict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all of us could see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could your neighbours in Ahmici see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, I would ask that Mr. Nobilo permit the witness time to answer the question before he asks the next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. You have to think about the interpreters, Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Yes, I am sorry. We must slow down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not know, I was not in Ahmici. They knew in the morning, they saw what was happening. If they went out of Ahmici, they must have seen the machine-guns, the reinforcements made of sandbags, and that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could they see the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This truck with the weapons, from what direction did it come?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It came from Busovaca.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, you mentioned three Mercedes. Could you explain to the judges, when you say a Mercedes, do you mean a limousine?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You mean with the HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The ordinary passenger car.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where did they come from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They came one of them from Busovaca and the other two from the direction of Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The killing of Patkovic, did you yourself see him being killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I did not see him the moment he was killed, but I saw them turning him round because I recognised his sweater and his coat, because we were sitting in the room with his friend.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you did not see under which circumstances he was killed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: By the sound of the bullet, I think it must have been a pistol.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned some neighbours who protected you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell me their names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was Igor, what his surname was, then there was someone Slavko and other Croat neighbours. There is nothing I can say against any one of them. It was all being done by army coming from the outside.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And these Croat neighbours, Igor, Franjo's son, were they wearing uniforms and they had HVO insignia too?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they did, but they did not do any evil to anyone as far as I know. I do not know about any others.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Tell me, before going to the school in Vitez, were there any problems with Cicko?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. He wore a black uniform, he had the letter U on his hat, he had the HVO patch on his sleeve and the chequer board flag and the U. He came and he cursed my Muslim mother, that he wants to -- that he is thirsty for Muslim blood, he took out a knife or a bayonet ready to slaughter and I nearly fainted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But who saved you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Franjo's wife and son. They somehow came from behind his back and pulled him away and then some locals, also HVOs, came and they would not let him do anything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did they, those HVO soldiers, did they tell you that you were to be taken to the school in Vitez because you would be safer there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he said we should not go near the window just in case a bullet may find its way there by chance.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Igor in the HVO, a military policeman?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was. His family would give us food during the night so that nobody knew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about Dervis Ahmic's house, did it remain in one piece?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, both Sefka's and his house were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you hear of Tihomir Blaskic in Jajce?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That is all, thank you, Mr. President. We have completed our cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Harmon, do you have any additional questions you would like to ask?

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, I now turn to my colleagues. Judge Riad?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I just want to have some clarifications about the things you said. Among the things you said, you said that you noticed when you were going I think to Vitez to see your doctor, you saw sandbags put to make shelters in the road towards Zenica and in the intersections near the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was this because of any attack coming on Vitez? Did you notice that anybody was attacking Vitez? Why did you think these sandbags were being put?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were putting there, as far as we could see, it was a preparation of the HVO to go against the army, but where the army was, where this military was, that I did not know, so they were making covers or shelters for themselves. They had the machine-guns there, those bandoleers, and we knew what was going to happen, that they were going against the Muslim population. It was all obvious, nothing was hidden there. I was going to Vitez even before that and nothing was there, but it was just around the time when they were making these preparations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But you could not see any threat which justified these preparations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, just the things that we were going to be taken to Busovaca, to Kordic, to be exchanged, nobody, everybody was going to be exchanged, I do not know. In terms of the neighbours, there were no threats from the neighbours, just from the HVO who were from somewhere else. Our neighbours were not bad towards us, they were really nice, they were fine towards us. I have nothing against them. I can only speak of what I have seen and what I did not know of I am not going to say anything. I received a big shock from all this.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How long before, let us say, the action against the civilians started, did these sandbags and preparations being put? Was it just before the attacks against the civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, several days before. I may not even have -- I could have not even seen it had I not gone to the doctors for the check-up. That is how I saw they were preparing. It was immediately clear to us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that you saw the HVO distributing weapons. Whom were they distributing the weapons to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were some people who were not locals, because otherwise I would have recognised them, because we were fine with them at first, and later too, with the locals we were fine. They had these camouflage uniforms, you know, the trousers, and on top they were in civilian clothes. They were going up towards upper Nadioci. I guess that is where they connect to Ahmici, through the forest. That is what I saw.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also saw bodies floating in the Lasva river, you saw three civilians tied together. Where were they coming from, could you notice where they were coming from and going where? Did you notice the source of these people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was coming up stream from Vitez, so there is Vitez and the river is flowing down from there. That is where they were coming. Where they were thrown in, dumped into the river, that I do not know. We just heard shooting, so pistol fire and other fire, so it was all near. Then later I saw three bodies and after I saw the second group of three bodies, it was over for me. I was in such a terrible shape that I came -- I was only 45 kilograms, I weighed only 45 kilograms. This was all from fear, not because of the lack of food, because our neighbours the Croats gave us food. They were very nice people. There was one man called Slavko and he said, "please, just gather and leave, flee towards the woods". He told us this, he was a very nice man.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did he tell you why, why you should flee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It so happened that you saw Petkovic being taken out and you said you heard him being shot --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: From the house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was his position? Was he one of the leaders of the area? Why did they choose him, or was he just taken as they would take anybody else? The same question, when they came in your house and hit you and your husband, was your husband among the people acting against the Croats?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, my husband was a retiree, he went into retirement before the war, his health was impaired. Patkovic came from Zenica to visit his daughter in Nadioci. He came to visit her. I do not know why him, he was no politician, he did not wear a uniform. I do not know if he had been a soldier before, but they took him out, that is all. They also wanted to take the Dervis Ahmic's son, but they hid him and he survived. They were nice people, so they sheltered some Muslims and these were the neighbours. Those who came from other sides from Skutjure, Dalmatia and Croatia, those were the bad people. That is it. What I did not see I cannot speak to, and I have no interest in lying. I feel sorry for General Blaskic, he is a young man, it is clear who sent him there, it is clear who is responsible for this there. I feel sorry for everyone, it was all kind of naive the way it all came, the people and the military, all that. It is sad all this that happened for all these lives.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to go back to my question, you have been hit and your husband hit and Petkovic has been killed, but that was for no special reason, you were not selected, so you were just taken as anybody else for no special reason, so there was no selection of people among others?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, and nobody else except for Patkovic. They took our refugee ID and they saw we were from Jajce. As far as I can recall, one of them could have been from the Jajce area, he was a HVO man, he had a hat on his head and he said, "it is all right", when he saw where we were from, that we were from Jajce and that was it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where are you living now? Where do you live? Do not answer that. You did not go back?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You spoke of your weekend house and so on. You never went back to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who occupies it now, do you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I know, these are all Croats, Croat refugees, there is a lot of Croat refugees. A lot of weekend houses were also burned down and otherwise destroyed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No Muslims are left, you mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, no Muslims left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RIAD
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Witness S, would I be interpreting your position correctly if I said that I understand you to be speaking with sadness but not with bitterness about what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, with sadness. I am sorry that all this happened. We had fine neighbours, both sides, we all lived well, and now hatred has entered the people. We were killed, we have nothing left. Fortunately nobody in my family was in the army, I was nobody in the military. This includes my brothers and my husband and my in-laws, but the families who lost people and only one member of the family surviving, that is really sad. That is terrible pain which will never go away.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had some good Croat neighbours and friends?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who protected you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you still in touch with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I would pass through Vitez, and only I would be afraid of Cicko. I am only afraid of him, of nobody else. I believe that we would all be glad to see each other, to hug and kiss each other, with all these neighbours. But in my family, there are all three ethnic groups, Croats and Serbs and we are Muslim, and everything was normal and we interact normally among ourselves.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Since these incidents happened, have you been back to the area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I just pass through, going to Sarajevo, when I was taking my husband to the hospital.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Some people mentioned to you the name of Mr. Kordic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had television in your home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, after we became refugees, no. I had everything in my original house, but during the war, no, we did not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us speak of your original home. Did you have television there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had it, I had everything, I had a fully furnished house. I could live normally and I could have lived like that to the end of my life. I did not miss anything, we were both retired, we went on vacations, we went to the coast.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you look at television then in your original home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We had not heard of Kordic until we became refugees, until the October 1992 we were in Jajce, you see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I see. Now let us talk about the sandbags. You said you visited Vitez and I gathered that you saw some sandbags at the intersection of the Hotel Vitez.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, not only on that intersection, it was in other intersections as well, towards the old Vitez as well, where the Muslims were, and over on the other side towards Zenica, it is called Treskavica. I saw all that. I had not seen it before, because I often went doctors, my wounds were not healing properly so I was getting them dressed. So I had not seen it before, until these preparations started about a week before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Somewhere in your evidence, you referred to these sandbags as "reinforcements". Would you describe the sandbags which you saw at the intersection at the Hotel Vitez as reinforcements?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I can describe that, of course. Everybody knows what a bag is, and they were stacked on top of one another and that was -- and then where the barrel was pointing out, that would leave a space as they were stacking these bags.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you see a gun barrel at that intersection?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course I did, I saw the whole machine-gun, I saw the bandoleers and the automatic rifles and I saw sniper rifles, I know this. I had a neighbour in Jajce, his name was Goran and at his house there were weapons. We went along well. The husband was a policeman, and they went to Dalmatia and they left the keys with me so I saw all these weapons in their house. When the Chetniks arrived, we just fled and left everything.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Could I trouble you to go back to that particular sandbag reinforcement which you saw at the Hotel Vitez intersection? You said you saw a gun. Could you tell the court, in what direction was the barrel pointed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This barrel was pointed -- it was not one machine-gun, there were two of them, they were pointing towards the old section of Vitez where exclusively Muslims, Bosniaks, lived, and up towards Vjetrenica, they trained their barrels towards Vjetrenica. I saw all this and I told my husband, "let us flee while we can, while the road is still open", and he said, "let us stay, even if we are killed".

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: One last question, --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: If I knew I would have left him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You saw all of this before 16th April?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: You are welcome.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you. The Tribunal is very appreciative for your having come to The Hague. I am sure this was not easy. I will not ask any additional questions.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not that hard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We were received very nicely here too, I have an impression that they were very, very nice to us, so when I go back to Jajce, they are all welcome to my place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. No, please do not move. The hearing will be adjourned until 4.30. (4.10 pm) (A short break) (4.30 pm)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Have the accused brought in, please. (Accused brought in)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Mr. Gregory Kehoe, I see you are the one who is going to do the examination. You were able to synthesise everything yesterday and I see you want to sustain your good reputation. The floor is yours, now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, thank you, your Honours. The next witness is Witness R. In an effort, Mr. President, your Honours, to comply with the Chamber's request, we have honed down our witness list and the witness for the village of Donje Veceriska. If we can turn to the ELMO just briefly, gentlemen, up in the booth, one can see that Donje Veceriska is the village where the pointer is pointed to and it is just above the village of Besici. What is in between there on the low level ground is the SPS factory, a factory that builds military wares. This particular village was attacked, as were many other villages in the Lasva Valley area, on 16th April 1993. This particular witness, Witness R, will detail that attack, the burning of houses, the killing of civilians, the ultimate removal of all the Muslims from the village on the morning of the 16th. He will likewise testify about the various units that were involved. Again he will testify of HV units, HVO units, units that were dressed in camouflage, units that were dressed in black, units that were dressed with the letter U, Ustasha, on their helmets. In addition to that he will testify that in addition to the burning of the housing on the 16th, that burning continued through the 17th and yet still on the 18th when the refugees from the village of Donje Veceriska fled to the UN base, which, you will see from the map, and I know your Honours have seen before, is down on the road going into Vitez. When they were in there with numerous other refugees, they were being sniped at, they could observe the continued burning of the village of Donje Veceriska on the 18th and we will have a photograph of that, the witness will be able to identify the locations that continued to be burned, and thereafter, consistent with the witness that testified this morning, Ms. Hrustic, he will testify that they observed the shelling of the village of Gacice from the low plain where the SPS factory was which, of course, was controlled by HVO troops. In sum, Mr. President, your Honours, that is what Witness R will testify to. With regard to relation to the charges itself, Mr. President, his testimony will cover virtually every paragraph in count 1. His testimony will go to the very heart of the persecution count, which is the persecution of the Muslim population in the Lasva Valley and elsewhere. His testimony will likewise be directed toward the wilful killing of civilians and as you note in counts 11 and 13 of the indictment, the destruction and plunder of property lists the village of Donje Veceriska as one of the villages where there was extensive destruction and destruction of property at the hands of soldiers under the command of the accused. That in substance, Mr. President, your Honours, is the testimony of Witness R and how it relates directly to the terms of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You see that only took three or four minutes. The Tribunal would really appreciate it if in all of your questions you could bring them back to these counts, which you generally do. All right, without any further ado, I can ask the Registrar to have the usher bring the witness in.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: If I may, your Honour, I think in an effort to expedite matters, at the outset, if I could offer him some of the exhibits that Defence counsel and certainly your Honours can follow along so that I will not have to interrupt him, he can go and explain what these numbers are and I think it is going to be a lot easier --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: That would be very good.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: -- than have him do a narrative and me come back to these numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: I think my colleagues will agree to that way of working. Very well, I think that is good (Witness entered court)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Witness R, do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: The Registrar is going to give you a declaration which you will be asked to read. It is the oath that you are to take before the judges. We are listening to you. Go ahead. Please read it. WITNESS R (sworn)

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please verify on the paper that the Registrar is showing you, but without stating your name, just be sure that it is your name. Do not say anything, simply say that is who you are.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You have protective measures which have been suggested by the Prosecutor and which the judges agreed to, in agreement with the Defence. You can speak without fear, and make your statement about the events that you experienced in Donje Veceriska at the time of the attack of 16th April 1993. We have discussed with the Prosecutor how this will be done, the Prosecutor will explain it to you, the floor is yours, Mr. Kehoe. Examined by MR. KEHOE

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon, Witness R.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, can you tell us your age at this point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am 39.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you a Muslim, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, prior to 16th April 1993, did you and your family live in the village of Donje Veceriska in the municipality of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before, Witness R, we get into your explanation and your narrative to the judges about what happened, you assisted the Office of the Prosecutor in preparing several maps and circled various locations that took place over the course of 16th April to 18th April, did you not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this juncture, Mr. Dubuisson, if we could give to the witness and to the judges and to the Defence Exhibit 161, 162 and 163, the first three maps. Those numbers should follow sequentially after number 12, going into the next and this should be the last one. May I, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead, in order to speed things up. Go ahead. Help the usher. Does the Defence see what is here? No, it is not clear for the Defence either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: It should follow sequentially, number wise. Thank you for the court's indulgence, Mr. President, your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well, let us go.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Now Witness R -- for the record, Mr. President, 161 and 162 are enlargements of Exhibit 55 and 163 is an enlargement of Exhibit 56. Witness R, you said that you were living in the village of Donje Veceriska until 16th April 1993, which was the morning of the attack, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your own words, Witness R, can you explain to the judges how you saw this conflict happening, beginning shortly before the attack on the 16th and then explain what happened with the attack, referring to the numbers on these exhibits and where you and the other Muslims from Donje Veceriska ultimately went to. Could you do that in your own words, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Let me begin my story by mid March 1993. The Croatian population started moving out, but they were only civilians, women, children and the elderly. They would move out and the next day they would come back to the village. On 15th April 1993, they did the same, they went away at dusk with vans, passenger cars, whatever they had, that is the Croatian civilians left, and then at 5.30 on the 16th, the attack by the HVO, by the Croats, was carried out against my village, Donje Veceriska. What happened was that at 5.30, my father and myself -- both my father and mother were killed -- we came out into the porch and we heard very strong shelling, we saw the shells fall all over the village. I followed my father into the house and when we got in, he told me that I should go and wake up Nevzeta Muslimovic and her children, she was a refugee from Turbe, she had four small children, and that I should wake her up and tell her to take shelter under the steps, though he thought that it was an air raid, because we had been raided before but by the JNA, so that everyone thought that the same thing was being repeated. However, I went out to Nevzeta's house, I ran across to the house. There was no infantry fire yet, no fire from infantry weapons, and as I was about to enter Nevzeta's house, I could see many soldiers near Milko Franjic's house, they were armed soldiers, HVO, Croats, and I jumped into the house. When I got in, this is building number 2 here (indicates), when I got in, the firing, the shooting intensified, children starting screaming, we all fell to the floor in the kitchen of Nevzeta Muslimovic's house and the bullets were coming through the walls. All the panes were broken by the bullets, it was chaos everywhere, screaming, crying. We were on the floor, and then HVO soldiers threw in a grenade, into the corridor. There was a very powerful explosion in the corridor, we were on the floor of the kitchen. After that, Nevzeta asked her husband to go upstairs to bring some money that her sister had sent her, I do not know how much exactly, about 200 German Marks, and when he came down the steps, he yelled, "flee, they have thrown another grenade". At that moment, I jumped, I picked up the smallest child who was three years old, I ran out of the house, there was a cloud of smoke and dust, and then another grenade went off, but fortunately it went off under the steps, so a piece of concrete hit me in the chest. I could hardly breathe. When I went out of the house, the children had followed their mother and their father, and when I got up, I could see many soldiers around us, some of them were wearing camouflage uniforms with helmets, with the letter U; others had black uniforms and they were masked. They also bore the letter U. Those with masks had HVO insignia too, they were cursing and insulting us and mentioning our balija mothers, and one of them hit me with a rifle butt. He told me to put my hands up behind my head, I know his name, he was Sulaja, he is the waiter's son. I also recognised Vlado Franjic, Milko Franjic, others were with masks and I could not recognise them. These I knew because they were my neighbours. They told me to put my hands on my head, and I did so. Then I had to go out into the road. There was shooting everywhere, all the houses and stables were on fire and behind us, behind this house where I was, everything was burning and I learnt later that Dzafer Basic from Obrovac had burnt in that house. He was a refugee. He was burnt together with a horse and a cow in the stable. When I got on to the road, the soldiers followed me, the HVO soldiers, and Dzemo Haskic's daughter called me out. She was two metres from the road. She called me by name to help, because the father was seriously wounded, the man had lost his arm, he was lying in the corridor in a pool of blood. Mechanically I went in that direction to help the man, but they were yelling at me, telling me to come back and cursing my mother, and so I decided if they were going to kill me, let them and I started to run between a tractor and Dzemo's old house, which is here marked with number 4 (indicates). I jumped over a fence, there was fire following me, then another fence, and when I reached Omer Haskic's stable, there was some shelter there. Omer's stable was burnt down. Haskic's house, stable, everything, there was flames everywhere, the cows were screeching, everything had been burnt down. When I reached the corner of the stable, the last bit of it, the last bit of the roof caved in. When I looked around again to run, I saw Bono Drmic with a rifle. He looked at me, we went to school together. He turned round, he cursed, I do not remember exactly what, and then he went, he left. So I took advantage of the moment and ran away, I fled to behind a concrete wall, where manure was piled. This was near the structure marked 6. I was sheltered there, and there was firing everywhere. I did not know where to go. I was trying to reach the lower parts of the village where most of the Muslims were, but the shooting was fierce, so I waited there for a chance to come and while I was waiting, I was barefoot, and I must have cut my foot on glass, because I did not feel any pain or anything. I saw two soldiers going towards Meho's house in camouflage uniforms. One of them had a helmet. There were several of them around the house, but I recognised by the colour of his hair Franjo Sapo, Sapina. They called Meho by name. He was a man of 65, he was a retiree. He was just about to light a cigarette. We just heard the burst of fire and the man dropped in a pool of blood. This was about six or seven metres away from me. After that, I ran across the road and entered a kind of summer kitchen near Meho's house which was full of children and women, they were crying, there was screaming. Again I found Nevzeta and her children there. They had fled there, but we could not stay, because they were approaching too close, and they were torching everything on the way. There was a blind man with us, a refugee from Turbe, so we carried him too, and all of us moved from that summer kitchen through an open area under fire into the house of Cazim Haskic. For the hour that we spent there, during that time, more than 50 or 40 to 50 grenades fell in that hour, in addition to infantry fire and anti-aircraft fire. We were in a cellar where there was water up to the knees. There was a new-born baby there, he was only 20 days old, he was Meho's grandson. There were many children. They were crying. However, we could not go further, so we hid there all that day,, because there was an open space in front of us, point 10 on the map, so there was no way that we could cross this area, and Dzafer, who had burnt in his stable that I mentioned at the beginning, and his wife was hit by a sniper coming from Zoran Franjic's house. It was 8.00 or 8.30 in the morning and no one dared go up to her and next to her was her little girl, who was two or three, and she was crying. Somehow we cried out to her that she should tie the wound up with something, because no one dared go up to her, because she was exposed to fire by HVO soldiers, and the Croats, the local Croats. It was only in the evening that we were able to help Hadzira. We made, improvise some stretchers. This was in the evening, and we carried her to the lower part of the village known as Brdo. There we established contact with people, they were mostly Muslim inhabitants there because all the Croats had left, except for the able-bodied men. So we got in touch with the people, they helped us, they gave us whatever they had to give. I did not want anything because my parents had been left behind, they were killed by the HVO soldiers. My father was 72, my mother also 72. My mother was disabled. Hadzira was later taken away by UNPROFOR to a hospital, I suppose. We stayed around in those houses during the 17th, and during the night, between the 17th and 18th, we decided to take another road leading out of Veceriska towards the UNPROFOR base and we decided to do this in the early morning between 3.00 and 4.00. We were completely silent. There was a column of 800 or more people, because there were many people who had fled from Karaula and Turbe. I have to mention that here at point 6 another three old women were killed, Habiba Haskic, who was 80, and her sister, who had fled from Karaula about the same age, maybe a couple of years younger, and Habiba's daughter-in-law, Hurabiba, who was 55. As we were going towards the base, and withdrawing from the village, at a curve, at a bend in the road, in the direction of the UNPROFOR base, the HVO shot at the civilians from the gates of the SPS factory, plant P, and from a hilltop known as Divjak. I have to point out that these were all civilians coming from Besici, they too had retreated to Brdo on the 17th in the evening, so that the whole village was there and we had to abandon the village because we were totally surrounded. There were quite a number of wounded civilians, and we had to retreat towards the UNPROFOR base. We were looking for salvation, we had nowhere else to go. The UNPROFOR met us, they switched on the lights, we all cried out that they should turn off the lights because they would shoot. When they saw us, they put us up in front of their battalion base, and we stayed there for four days, maybe five, I cannot remember, because I was extremely upset because of my parents, who were left behind in the house and were later killed by the HVO soldiers, and they are buried in a joint grave in old Vitez. While we were there next to the UNPROFOR base at Divjak, Divjak was attacked too and the civilians had withdrawn, the Muslim civilians, and they were all put up there because we felt that they could protect us, as we were all civilians. On the 18th, I think it was in the afternoon, the explosion occurred, that terrible explosion in Stari Vitez so that there were very many people who came to the base, because the UNPROFOR was evacuating the women and children, so that night, the night of the 18th, near the improvised camp, four civilians, they were firing bullets at us and again there were cries and screams but fortunately no one was wounded. Maybe they were, but I cannot remember, I do not know. Then the UNPROFOR soldiers found the two men who were shooting, I saw them escorting them in camouflage uniforms, they were saying something, I do not know what. I must mention that in Veceriska, eight civilians were killed, mostly women and elderly people, and also Sakib Zlotrg, who was over 65. While we were surrounded in Donje Veceriska, throughout the chemical plant, the SPS, the Vitezit, there was an anti-aircraft gun mounted on a car, and it was shooting at houses and setting fire to them. It would fire from one end and then go by the other side so that it was firing while moving, and there was total chaos. I do not myself know how I survived, because I nearly went mad, altogether mad. That is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay, Witness R --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness R. I think that the Prosecutor will ask for some details about several points in support of the indictment against General Blaskic. Mr. Kehoe?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Just a few questions, Witness R. Prior to 16th April, where were you working?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was working in the SPS in Vitez, the Princip factory.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did there come a time in 1993 when special units, special armed units came into the SPS factory and essentially took control?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This was as early as October 1992, before the new year's. They came in, I did not know them, they just entered the factory, they took over, there was no resistance there, nobody was putting up any resistance, anyway. When we would arrive at work, we would see these unknown soldiers. I had never seen them before. They had the HVO insignia. I even saw the HV insignia, because I had to pass by them at the gate to enter. At Christmas and new year, they also shot at our houses from this Vitezit compound, we call it Princip. They partied there, they behaved as if it was their own. They put up the HVO flags at the gates of this factory, they would often come to Veceriska, these special troops, they used to call them the special troops and this three-barrelled anti-aircraft gun would be paraded around. It was psychological, to intimidate the people, the Muslim population. They would pass by my house as well.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, you said that these soldiers had HV patches as well as HVO patches, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, did these soldiers participate in the attack on the village of Donje Veceriska on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When I was taken prisoner in front of this house, I saw all kinds of insignia. There were a lot of soldiers in black with this letter U painted on and then there was HV and there were all kinds of insignia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just explain to the judges, what kind of insignias did you see when you were taken prisoner on the morning of the 16th, in addition to the U?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Except for the U, I saw -- I cannot remember which arm it was on, it was on the camouflage uniforms. There were the HVO patches and they had ribbons around. I think that they were blue, I cannot recall the colour. They had their faces painted too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prior to the attack as well, Witness R, were there any attempts by the local HVO to disarm the Muslim population?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, after the first conflict, I cannot recall because -- I cannot recall precisely when this was, but the same day, they came not only to us but in the whole municipality, asking that everybody surrender their weapons, what everyone had.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many attempts were there for you to surrender those weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I recall that one, there may have been more but I do not remember.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, let me turn your attention to the evening of 15th April 1993, and I ask you, were you home watching television?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, on 15th April I was at home with my late parents and I was watching TV, and on TV, I do not remember what time, some time late at night, not very very late, I watched a press conference, I do not know, from that area. I do not know the name of that press conference, it was a HVO thing. I saw Kordic, I saw the present gentleman, and Ignjac Kostroman. I heard Kordic say -- I was not that interested in what he was saying, but he said, "brother Croats, the moment has come". I guess that was a signal for them for the attack.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, when you say the present gentleman was there as well, who are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: General Blaskic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, was there a TV conference the same day that the Croats from your village vacated Donje Veceriska and went up to Gornji Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, 15th in the evening of the 15th, that is exactly when it was, on the 15th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If I could turn your attention and just ask you several questions concerning the chart that is right in front of you, Exhibit 161, to your right hand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: That is it. Just so we can clarify -- counsel, there is an extra copy up here. I think they gave two to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYMAN
utterances.text: That explains our confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Can we go through these numbers, Witness R, and can you just explain to the judges these particular numbers. Number 1 is your house, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is where your mother and father were murdered --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Where they were killed, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question, I am sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: It is okay, you answered the question, we can move on. Number 2 is the house that you fled to that morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, and where I was taken prisoner. Number 3 is the house of Milko Franjic, where I saw that soldier and Milko Franjic and they went down to the road. Dzemo Haskic's house is 4, where Dzemo was badly wounded. Number 5 is where the stable of Omer Haskic, and 6 is where I hid behind that concrete wall, where the manure was. Number 7 is the spot where Meho Haskic was killed in front of his house. Number 8, where I found a lot of women and children in the summer kitchen, so it is -- Mahmut Haskic's summer kitchen. Number 9 is Cazim Haskic's house where we hid in the basement. Number 10 is where Hadzira was wounded and where she was lying wounded. Number 11 is Zoran Franjic's house, from which they fired at Hadzira, and 12 is where the headquarters of the HVO were, that is Drmic's house.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned several individuals who were shot that morning that you observed, Dzemo Haskic, Meho Haskic and Hadzira Bacic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Bacic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Bacic. Were those three people all Muslims?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were all Muslims.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned that there were a series of houses burning when you came out of house number 2 and you were taken prisoner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, all the houses along the road behind me were on fire, when I came to the road I saw everything burning. Then below at number 6, it was all in flames.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, were these Muslim houses on fire or were they Croat houses on fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those were Muslim houses, all of them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When this attack was taking place, you told the judges that you saw soldiers in and around Milko Franjic's house, number 3.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, number 3. There were a lot of them. Below this house where these trees were, you can see it well in the drawing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many soldiers did you see during the course of that day? How many HVO soldiers and HV soldiers did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only around the house at Nevzeta Muslimovic's. I think I saw 50 or 60 soldiers, that is my estimate, maybe there were even more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, how many soldiers did you see over the course of that day going through Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I did not understand the question very well. You mentioned 16th April?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No, on the day of the attack, on the whole day.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I saw a lot of soldiers, a whole of soldiers, I do not know the exact number, but a lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you give an estimate, 200, 300?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe, there was a lot of them, just around the house where I was, there were 50 or 60 and maybe even more, and as I was fleeing, they were milling all around these houses, so there were more.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Witness R, you mentioned soldiers in camouflage uniforms, you mentioned soldiers in black uniforms, you mentioned soldiers with HVO patches, you mentioned soldiers with HV patches, you mentioned soldiers with an U on their side, you mentioned soldiers with helmets with an U. Were all of these soldiers working together?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course they were working together. They were all attacking.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The last point before we get off this map was house number 12. Whose house is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the HVO headquarters in Veceriska, and it was Franjo Drmic's house too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At any time shortly before the attack, did you see any unusual activity around that house?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Before the attack itself, I could not because my house was far away, so we did not know, we could not see.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told the judges that you fled towards the area of Brdo from the house that is located at point 9, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next map, which is Brdo, and that is the next map, 162. If I could ask the usher's assistance? It is this map, Mr. Usher (indicates). You said that you fled in the evening of the 16th going into 17th April, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we established contact when we moved Hadzira there, on the 17th in the evening.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the area that you describe as Brdo circled with a number 15 next to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also mentioned, sir, that later on other Muslims from the area of Besici came to your area in Brdo, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is marked with 16. That is Besici. They all came there in order to make an agreement and then we all pulled out and we walked in silence. It may have been 1,000 people in the column, because there were a lot of refugees, children, women, the elderly, everyone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now Witness R, just to ask you a couple of questions about the anti-aircraft weapon that you said was shooting at you from the -- you and the other Muslim civilians from the SPS factory. Can I ask you to take a look at the place at the top with a number 17 and towards the left with the number 18?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you see those locations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do see them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are those the approximate locations where this anti-aircraft weapon shot at you and the other Muslim civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you or any of the other civilians have an anti-aircraft weapon to return fire?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We did not have anything, maybe there was some hunting rifles, because the aggression in Herzegovina was already in progress and there was a front-line at Turbe and Visoko, where we were attacked by the Serbian and Montenegrin aggressors, because we never expected that our neighbours would attack us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just let me complete this map, there is an area -- was there shelling taking place into your area of the village and then the other parts of the village from a place that you called Hum?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What number is that marked on the map?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is marked with number 13.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of shells were being fired from the Hum area number 13 into the village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mortar shells, an anti-aircraft gun, the abbreviation is locally PAT, and all kinds of things.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So during the course of the 16th, Witness R, there was shelling coming from point 3 as well as from the SPS factory on 17 and 18; points 13, 17 and 18?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we finish with this, the area that is over on the right-hand side of the map, number 19, what location is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is the target area, for target practice area, where the HVO soldiers were getting their training. They were often doing target practice there and exercises.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Before we complete this area of questioning and go on to the next map, Witness R, you mentioned that there were HVO soldiers that you personally recognised that participated in the attack against you, those that you named.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You also said that there were soldiers that you did not know, is that not right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is right, there were some who I did not know at all, who were not from the Vitez municipality or from that area at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Witness R, that HVO, HV soldiers from both in the Vitez area and outside the Vitez area joined together to attack Donje Veceriska on the morning of 16th April 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They joined together to attack, not only Veceriska but the entire municipality of Vitez, with the exception of maybe ...

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have a few other items to go, I think this is probably an appropriate place to break, if your Honour sees fit. We do have quite a bit more to go through, because this is our only witness on this village.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We shall stop at 5.45 since we began at 2.45, so we still have about 15 minutes left. We could continue until 5.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. President. Would it have been approximately 3.00 or 4.00 on the morning of the 18th that you went and moved towards UNPROFOR, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the map before you, Exhibit 162, there is a road marked in green with a number 20 next to it. Is that the road that you took?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we took that road, all of us.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, let me turn your attention to the last map, which is Exhibit 163.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have found it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is that road again, and this is a portion of Exhibit 56, is that road again marked in green and marked with the number 20, going down to the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned as well, Witness R, that as you were heading down that road -- and it was dark out, was it not, at 3.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it was dark, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned that you were being shot at from two locations, one being a location in the SPS factory and the other on the other side of the road, but those have been marked as approximately numbers 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The village that the UNPROFOR base is located in, what is the name of that little hamlet?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was called Divjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Likewise, have we segregated that area aside with the number 23 that includes a portion of the village of Divjak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was Divjak also attacked by the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we got to the UNPROFOR base, they immediately left, everyone ran away towards the UNPROFOR base, so that Divjak was taken immediately.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Who ran away towards the UNPROFOR base?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The civilian population of Divjak, because the fire was moving in their direction, so they fled, they had nowhere to go, because they all thought that they could save their lives if they reached the base.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are these Muslim civilians or Croat civilians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Only Muslims, only Muslim population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said you went and moved towards the UNPROFOR base; that is circled with number 24, is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you likewise receive some incoming sniper fire from houses close by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, we were being sniped at from nearby houses, because there was a mixture of Muslim and Croat houses there, and they were also firing over the improvised camp so as to frighten the civilians or for some other reason, I do not know. But the UNPROFOR members managed to catch two of them and bring them to the base. What they did to them I do not know, whether they had any discussions with them, but I know that later on they were not there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The places that you were being sniped at from, would that have been -- was that circled with the area of number 25?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, as you were located in the area on the UNPROFOR base and 25, did you continue -- could you see the village of Donje Veceriska from where you were?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, because it is relatively close, maybe two kilometres, or less, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you looked up there, what did you see?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We could even see soldiers. The village was burning, everything was in flames, but mostly the Muslim houses. Everything was on fire. We could see that the conflicts were of very extreme intensity.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At this point, when the fires were taking place in these houses, were all the Muslims out of village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, they were all outside the village, because we were all by then in front of the UNPROFOR base at Divjak.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say, Witness R, that two days after the attack, 18th April, soldiers, HVO soldiers are still burning Muslim houses in Donje Veceriska?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there are even photographs of this, showing the houses burning. People were crying as they watched their houses burning on the 18th, the afternoon of the 18th. That was exactly the day when that explosion occurred.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, let us turn to those photographs. With the assistance of the Registrar, if we could turn to a series of photographs, I think it is Exhibit 166. Mr. Dubuisson, it is this one first, okay? We could use this on the ELMO. If we could turn to that top photograph right there, that is the first one which is 166/1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: For the record, the source of this photograph, Mr. President and your Honours, is the Cheshire Battalion and it is a photograph that was taken shortly before the conflict. Witness R, you mentioned that an anti-aircraft weapon had been used in the SPS factory during 16th April 1993. I ask you, looking at this photograph, do you recognise this particular vehicle with this anti-aircraft weapon on it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course. This is it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How do you know that is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because prior to the conflict, I saw this vehicle. They drove it around to intimidate the people. These unknown people who had HV and HVO insignia. They wanted us to see that they had such weapons. Many of us had never even seen any such thing before.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know where this photograph is taken, sir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, the photograph was taken in front of the former building of the SUP, the Federal Ministry of the Interior in Vitez.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Witness R, where is that in relation to the Hotel Vitez?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is across the street, across the street from the Vitez hotel.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us turn to the next photograph --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Since there are many photos and the interpreters are tired, as is the witness, it is now 5.45, and we will begin tomorrow morning at 10.00. The court stands adjourned, we will start again tomorrow at 10.00. (5.45 pm)

procedural_notes.text: (Hearing adjourned until 10.00 am the following day)
